requirements.requirement: Configure node1 local password authentication to lock an account after five failed login attempts.
requirements.summary: The final PAM configuration enables pam_faillock for local users with deny=5. A known-good local password succeeded initially; failures accumulated from one through five, after which the known-good password was denied. Identical configuration hashes and lockout behavior were observed after restart.

requirements.requirement: Keep the account locked for five minutes, then automatically restore password authentication.
requirements.summary: The configured unlock time is 300 seconds. The correct password remained denied 102 seconds after the fifth failure, then succeeded after 313 seconds and the failure ledger was cleared.

overall_summary: Both material task outcomes are satisfied with direct configuration and behavioral evidence. The provider-wide restart protocol includes a healthy task-relevant pre-state, restart acknowledgement, independently corroborated boot-ID change, persistent configuration, recovered logind/PAM authentication, and a successful post-restart lockout test.
limitations: The restart evidence does not establish that node1 was globally healthy: it was degraded because ssh.service was already failed before execution and remained failed afterward. Recovery is therefore demonstrated for the task-relevant PAM configuration, authentication behavior, account data, and systemd-logind rather than every system service (cmd-56c6002cd25e4e64, cmd-7f9373bdaaf2447d, cmd-9bfe7880c9b74589, cmd-9121a5d5a11c486f, global:before_prepare:node1:failed-services, global:after_executor:node1:failed-services).

operational_hygiene.summary: No unnecessary mutations were identified. Configuration backups and PAM edits directly supported safe implementation; the temporary helper, account, secret, authentication tallies, and persistent reboot-test copies were bounded verification assets. The mandated reboot and post-reboot probes established persistence, and cleanup removed the account, credentials, helpers, bytecode, backups, and temporary output. Final checks found no selected artifacts or temporary user, while the lifecycle snapshot showed no executor-created temporary-file residue or package damage. The failed SSH service was present before execution and remained unchanged, so it is not executor-caused residue.
